**Market Parameters Report – December 2008** 





### **1. Demand for platinum** 

- _After a heavy decline in 2008, demand for platinum is expected to stabilise with improvements in jewellery offsetting demand weakness in autocatalyst.  We have lowered our estimate for autocatalyst demand in 2008 and made sharp cuts to our forecast for 2009._

|Autocatalyst|4,262|3,959|3,452|3,450|

### **1.1  Autocatalyst** 

- The outlook for the global auto industry is deteriorating by the day, with a collapse in Q4 2008 sales in most major markets now feeding through to hefty cuts in production settings for 2009.  Given the speed and severity of this, we now expect a 3% decline in global vehicle production this year and a sharper 7% fall in 2009 as Europe and Japan join North America in suffering double‐digit year‐on‐year losses. 

- Our anticipated 15% decline in European vehicle production for 2009 will hit platinum especially hard owing to its heavy bias towards diesel (more than 50% of sales) which remains a platinum intensive application despite the increasing use of palladium. 

- Although some improvement in auto production is expected in 2010, this is unlikely to result in increased demand for platinum due to the countervailing forces of substitution in both gasoline and diesel applications and the ongoing effects of thrifting. 

### **1.2 Jewellery** 

- After a disast

rous year in 2008, we remain of the view that net demand for platinum in jewellery will recover strongly in 2009.  With prices remaining subdued, we expect further gains in 2010 but are not anticipating a return to the peak levels of earlier this decade, which would most likely require prices significantly below even today’s levels. 

### **1.3 Industrial** 

- We have raised our estimates for glass industry demand in 2008 to reflect capacity expansions in fibreglass production in China, although the scale of this is unlikely to be repeated in 2009 and 2010.  Meanwhile, the pace of expansion in LCD substrate capacity is slowing in the face of weakening panel demand.  This will have little effect on platinum demand in 2009 as most projects entering production next year are already well advanced. However, the outlook for 2010 is significantly worse as many new projects are expected to be postponed or cancelled as manufacturers seek to conserve capital.

### **2. Demand for palladium** 

- _The recent collapse in vehicle sales will lead to a sharp decline in global production in 2009 and a commensurate fall in palladium demand.  With little prospect of a step‐change in jewellery or other areas of demand, palladium is fully exposed to the turmoil now engulfing the global automotive industry but should improve from 2010 as the storm abates._

### **2.1 Autocatalyst** 

- Despite last ditch emergency loans to rescue General Motors and Chrysler from bankruptcy, this is unlikely to prevent a further decline in North American auto production in 2009. Contrary to earlier expectations, it now seems likely that this will be just as bad as the damage in 2008 when production is estimated to have fallen by 16%.  Adding in the prospect of heavy falls in Europe and Japan, we now expect demand for palladium in autocatalyst to contract sharply in 2009.  However, as production improves from 2010, we expect demand for palladium to recover quite strongly, aided further by substitution gains. 

### **2.2 Jewellery** 

- We maintain our estimates for 2008 and 2009 and expect further modest gains in 2010.  We have assumed the continuing absence of a major promotional campaign for palladium jewellery for the duration of the forecast period. 

### **2.3 Industrial** 

- With a weakening outlook for consumer electronic goods, we now see little scope for higher demand in electronics applications in 2009 and have adjusted our forecast accordingly. Sales of handheld devices are now expected to decline next year afte

r a period of multi‐year gains.  However, the effects of this should be offset by continued, albeit slower growth in personal computers and flat panel televisions until sales of handhelds recover in 2010.

### **3. Supply** 

### **3.1 Platinum supply** 

- _Cut‐backs in mine production are now emerging and we have lowered our forecast for 2009 considerably.  We now see minimal supply growth next year with recovery deferred until 2010.  However, prices have yet to improve and further cuts may soon become necessary._ 

|**Platinum 000 ozs**|**2007**|**2008E**|**2009F**|**2010F**|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|**Mineproduction:**|||||
|South Africa|5,075|4,585|4,702|4,928|
|Russia|917|793|770|765|
|Canada|197|218|187|262|
|United States|120|112|108|108|
|Zimbabwe|169|168|180|191|
|Others|97|117|110|112|
|**Total mineproduction**|**6,575**|**5,993**|**6,056**|**6,365**|
|Autocatalyst recycling|926|1,019|1,107|1,208|
|**Total supply**|**7,501**|**7,012**|**7,164**|**7,574**|



- During December, Anglo Platinum gave their first formal guidance of production for 2009 with a target of 2.4m ounces.  Although not billed as a cut, this is well below the market consensus of 2.7m ounces and includes the recovery of losses from the recent Polokwane smelter incident.  In addition, Aquarius announced the extended closure of the Everest mine in South Africa after geological difficulties halted production.  Although Aquarius has suggested mining may resume at Everest in the second half of 2009, we do not expect this to occur until the following year.  Meanwhile, Russia’s Norilsk Nickel announced lower than forecast production at its domestic operations and issued reduced guidance for 2009. 

- With these changes included, South Africa will show only minimal growth in 2009 and global mine production is likely to remain largely unchanged at a shade over 6m ounces of platinum.  By our estimate, this represents a cut of some 450,000 ounces from what might have been achieved under other circumstances.  Although significant, the lack of a positive price response up to now suggests outright cuts in global production may soon become necessary, rather than the steady‐state now intimated.  We should hear again from Amplats in February and await news from Impala in January. 

- Meanwhile, we are assuming moderate growth in South Africa’s production for 2010, although this too has been scaled back considerably from earlier estimates.  With an assist from autocatalyst recycling, this should lift total supply in 2010 to just over 7.5m ounces.

### **3.2 Palladium supply** 

- _With reduced production from Russia and South Africa, mine output of palladium will fall sharply in 2008, easing further in 2009.  Increased recovery from autocatalyst recycling will stabilise supply in 2009 before growth re‐emerges in 2010._

**2009F**|**2010F**|

|Autocatalyst recycling|963|1,225|1,521|1,845|
|**Total supply**|**7,998**|**7,597**|**7,662**|**8,257**|



- In a recent statement, Norilsk Nickel announced that palladium output in 2008 would be significantly below expectations and will fall still further in 2009.  With lower forecasts from South Africa and elsewhere, we have lowered our estimates for global palladium mine production over the forecast period, with reductions of 320,000 ounces and 737,000 ounces in 2008 and 2009 respectively. 

- Despite continuing growth in autocatalyst recycling, this will leave total supplies of palladium broadly unchanged in 2009, with growth reappearing in 2010 as mine production from South Africa rises moderately.  For 2010, we have assumed production from Russia will remain in line with Norilsk’s guidance for the previous year.

### **4. Market balances** 

### **4.1 Platinum** 

- _With supplies having reduced, we now estimate a small deficit for platinum in 2008 at the “gross” level and a modest surplus in 2009.  Given the degree of uncertainty over 2009, we see this currently as a balanced market in both years.  With supplies increasing and demand sluggish, we expect platinum to register a substantial surplus in 2010._ 

- _Investors in platinum ETFs are likely to have added nearly 100,000 ounces to their holdings in 2008, despite heavy liquidations over the second half of the year.  Although this enlarges platinum’s apparent deficit, this is not relevant to its underlying fundamentals or the scale of above‐ground stocks._

### **4.2 Palladium** 

- _Recent cuts in production have ensured that palladium remains in deficit at the “gross” level despite significantly lower demand estimates, especially for 2009.  This implies a continuing erosion of above‐ground stocks._ 

- _Sales of palladium from Russian government stocks are a continuing feature of this forecast and we have raised the level of sales expected in 2009 to reflect shipments into Switzerland in August/September of this year._ 

- _Unlike platinum, ETF investment in palladium has proven to be resilient and is set to post higher year‐on‐year net investment in 2008.  This appears likely to produce a residual deficit for palladium in 2009, the first for several years._

### **5. Above‐ground stocks** 

- _Above‐ground stocks are implied from historical trade data for Switzerland (dating from 1970) and declared stocks on the Nymex and Tocom futures exchanges.  Excluded are stocks held by governments (including Russia), producers, refiners and fabricators and consumers._ 

|**Implied stocks**|**2007**|**2008E**|**2009F**|**2010F**|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|**Platinum:**|||||
|Stock atyear end(million ozs)|1.39|1.37|1.50|1.92|
|Demand cover(months)|2.2|2.3|2.6|3.2|
|**Palladium:**|||||
|Stock atyear end(million ozs)|8.37|7.65|7.17|6.78|
|Demand cover(months)|12.1|10.6|9.3|8.3|



- Through to the end of 2009, above‐ground stocks of **platinum** are expected to rise marginally, with the effect of supply reductions largely negated by reduced estimates for demand.  However, with the addition of 2010 and a large surplus forecast for that year, stocks are expected to reach almost 2m ounces by that time, with demand cover rising above 3 months.  In the meantime, demand cover is expected to remain slender at slightly over 2.5 months by the end of 2009. 

- Recurring gross deficits for **palladium** will continue to erode above‐ground stocks and although these are forecast to remain substantial, we expect these to fall below 7m ounces by the end of 2010.  In terms of demand cover, stocks will decline from an equivalent of 12 months fabrication demand at the end of 2007 to a little over 8 months demand cover at the end of the forecast period. 

- Note: flows of palladium from Russian state stocks into Zurich have been excluded from the forecast years 2008, 2009 and 2010 (although these are known to have occurred already this year).  While these movements may cause Zurich stocks to rise, we have taken the view this will be matched by a corresponding decline in Russia’s holdings.
